newsitem.title: ITALY: Europe's "big five" to reassure Turkey on ties.
newsitem.headline: Europe's "big five" to reassure Turkey on ties.

text.p: Western Europe's "big five" powers will seek to reassure Turkey that they are committed to close ties when their foreign ministers meet on Wednesday against the backdrop of Greek-Turkish tension over Cyprus.
The Rome talks will bring the ministers of Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain together with Turkey's Tansu Ciller to review a relationship that has come under growing strains.

The fear among the five is that the Cyprus stand-off, coupled with Turkish frustration at lack of progress in its ties with the European Union, could push the Islamist-led government to turn to its Moslem neighbours and trigger frictions in NATO.
"We want to ensure that the gap between Turkey and Europe does not become too wide," a senior European diplomat said.
"We are hoping that this meeting will be accompanied by a blast of warmth and good feeling that Turkey at last feels it is being taken seriously," the diplomat added.

The five are likely to urge Turkey to lower the heat over Cyprus, where Greek Cypriot government plans to deploy Russian anti-aircraft missiles on the divided island have been met by Turkish threats of military retaliation.
"It's not going to help if they indulge in rhetoric. We need measures to reduce tension and restore a level-headed negotiating atmosphere," a British official said.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974, when Turkey invaded and occupied the northern third of the island after a Greek Cypriot coup engineered by Greece's then military government.
EU and NATO diplomats believe the crisis risks dragging Cyprus into the wider Greek-Turkish dispute and could complicate the search for an international settlement for the island.

EU countries are keen to achieve a solution this year ahead of the start of EU accession talks with Cyprus, probably in 1998, fearing that failure to settle the island's future could delay similar talks with other applicants from eastern Europe.
Turkey's annoyance at the logjam on its own aspirations for full EU membership has been increased by its perception that other countries appear to have jumped ahead of it in the queue.

Ciller's office said she would push in Rome for a clear signal that Turkey will not be overlooked, though European diplomats say no firm undertaking can yet be given and that Wednesday's talks are not within the EU framework.
"This time...we expect a clear answer to our membership request," a Turkish foreign ministry official said.
He said Ciller would also raise the issue of blocked financial aid to Ankara agreed under a customs union which went into effect at the start of 1996.
Turkey blames Greece for blocking the aid though there is also EU concern over Ankara's human rights record.

European governments fear the friction over EU issues could spill over into NATO. Diplomats say Turkey, an alliance member, is now hinting that it could block NATO decisions in retaliation, including planned enlargement eastwards.
There is also concern that Turkey, an important ally for the West because it borders volatile regions of the Caucasus and the Middle East, will look increasingly to the Moslem world.
"Turkey feels that it is wrongly treated by Europe," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said this month.
Greece, meanwhile, has made clear it opposes the Rome talks.

"We understand that some countries have special interests in Turkey but we don't feel it's right to have contacts outside the EU framework. They give the wrong impression to Turkey that there is no pressure on such issues as human rights," a senior Greek foreign ministry official said.
